claim: A frequency byte does not drive a formula and does not have a hundred and twenty-eight values. Its top four bits index a table of sixteen entries, so eight settings share each entry, and the entries are the named third octaves between the two frequencies the page prints against that address -- with one that is not. On 200 - 6.3k, fifteen of the sixteen sit within 0.07 octaves of 200, 250, 400, 500, 630, 800, 1k, 1.25k, 1.6k, 2k, 2.5k, 3.15k, 4k, 5k and 6.3k, a median 0.03 and under what a twelfth-octave reading resolves. The third entry sits at 279 Hz where the series says 315, which is 0.18 octaves and two bands, and it is the only entry the reading and the series disagree about. Both mid sections return that same 279, and they return the whole of the first four entries to within 0.002 octaves of each other, so the two index one table rather than two. Read across its own eight settings the entry does not move -- 279.1, 278.7, 278.8 and 279.0 at 16, 17, 20 and 23 -- and the settings either side of it return the entries either side, so the stride is eight and the number in the table is 279.
named: a third-octave coefficient table indexed by the byte's high nibble, with one entry that is not a third octave

measurements.read_as: The width byte of the same section, swept with the frequency byte held at 64. It is the control on the reading and not evidence about the table: a byte that changes how wide a feature is and not where it sits must leave a reading of where it sits alone. The fitted position holds inside 0.024 octaves while the window it was fitted over runs from four bands to forty-nine, and the largest band moves 0.167 octaves over the same settings -- so what the bottom three entries disagree by is not the feature's width being read as its place.

measurements.why: The width byte swept with the frequency byte at the bottom of its range. The top moves from 179 Hz at the width the table was first read at to 199 Hz two steps narrower, so a reading of this section at one width is a reading of that width's shape and not of the entry behind it.

The same width sweep at the middle of the frequency byte's range, which is the control the run above is read against: there the top holds inside 0.02 octaves over the same three widths. The width moves the peak at the bottom of the range and not at the middle, and that is measured rather than argued.

The whole table read at the narrowest width, one setting inside every one of the sixteen entries. The first reading of this table asked twelve settings that fall in ten entries, so six were never asked and were being assumed.
Four bytes across the third entry's own eight and the byte below it. A plateau measured at one byte is a point, and a boundary in the wrong place would look exactly like an entry in the wrong place.
The second mid asked at the same four entries at its own narrowest width. It returns 279 where the first does, which makes the entry the table's rather than one section's coefficients.

A low-pass corner swept across a printed range that begins one third octave above the one the mid table was read on, so its second entry is the same element of any shared list as the mid range's third. The chorus it sits in is turned into a filter and nothing else -- no pre-delay, no modulation, the balance fully across to the effect -- and the reference is the same chain with the pre-filter switched off, which is a corner's own null.

The same four settings read through the high-pass instead. Two filters that share nothing but the byte behind them, so a corner both agree on is a number in a table rather than a property of one filter.

The run this claim queued, made. A phaser's manual on the one printed range this unit has whose ends bracket a number of third octaves other than sixteen -- and the run is reported rather than read, because it measured that its own instrument does not work.

document_rows.read_as: Evidence that a page prints those two figures against those two addresses, and nothing about the unit. What the claim takes from them is the two ends of the table and not any entry between them: every entry here is a named third octave, which is a reading of the series and is the part a reader may disagree with.

era_priors.claim: A frequency parameter of this period is a table of filter coefficients indexed by the byte, not a frequency the part computes coefficients from.
era_priors.why: Turning a frequency into a biquad needs a sine and a tangent, which a small control processor of the era would run once per parameter change and would rather not. Storing the coefficients instead makes the entry expensive in memory, which is why the table is short where a rate table is not: a rate entry is one number and a filter entry is a set.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: Two settings inside one entry returned different frequencies at a resolution the run can tell apart, or the number of distinct values across the byte turned out to be near a hundred and twenty-eight.

era_priors.claim: A table's stride is a power of two, because dividing by one is a shift.
era_priors.why: A hundred and twenty-eight settings over sixteen entries is eight each. A table of twenty entries would need a divide or a second table, which is the reason the printed range that holds twenty third octaves is expected to behave differently and is the run this claim queues.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: The entry boundaries turned out not to fall on multiples of eight -- which is measurable at settings 6, 7, 8 and 9 and has not been asked.

community.claim: Read out of the program of Roland's own later software rendering of this line: a frequency parameter there carries no frequency but selects one of a short list of stored coefficient sets; a shelf's corner is a choice between two such lists rather than a setting that varies; a gain indexes a short table and a byte past its ends is ignored rather than clamped; and the list a frequency selects from is sixteen entries once the one slot that resolves to the selection's own fallback is counted out. What was read is a rendering written years after the hardware, carrying the material of three earlier units of this line and not of this one, so none of it is evidence about what this unit's table holds -- it is a second design of the same decade by the same maker, which is what the era prior above is made of and no more. It leans where the second alternative leans and settles nothing: that a parameter is a table in one design is silent on where another design's entries sit, and the run that would separate the two is the one already queued under what this does not close. It was read after this claim was made and after the records it rests on were published.
community.source: The TabulaSonora project's reverse-engineering record of the Roland SOUND Canvas VA voice: docs/FINDINGS.md in its spec repository, and the insertion-effect source of its NativeTS engine. Read 2026-09-13.

adds: Each record says which band the deviation was largest in at each setting it was asked at, where a curve fitted over the whole feature puts its top, and says in as many words that no filter, no corner and no order is in it. Nothing in any of them says the readings are entries of a table, that the table has sixteen of them, that eight settings share one, that the two mid sections share it, or that the entries are the third octaves the page's two ends bracket. That is the whole of what is added here, and it is added by holding five candidate laws against the same readings rather than by fitting one to them.

alternatives.reading: The entries are sixteen frequencies at equal ratios between the printed ends rather than the named third octaves. On a range whose ends bracket sixteen third octaves the two are the same series to within a third of a percent, and both ranges this claim has been read on are such a range.

separated_by.observable: Where the entries of a printed range fall whose ends bracket a number of third octaves that is not sixteen.

predicts.the named third octaves: The entries are third octaves whatever the range, so a range bracketing twenty of them either runs out before its printed top or does not step by eight settings.
predicts.equal ratios between the printed ends: The entries always divide the printed range into fifteen equal ratios, so on 100 - 8.0k they step by 0.42 octaves rather than 0.33.

separated_by.sensitivity_here: 0.09 octaves an entry, accumulating to 1.3 across the byte, against a reading that resolves 0.083.
separated_by.why_not_separable: This unit prints exactly one such range, 100 - 8.0k, and it prints it against a phaser's manual on six types and nothing else. That run was made and the record says why it cannot be read: four notches whose ratios to each other move with the setting, so no factor maps a notch to an entry. Nothing else on this machine has a frequency range that separates the two, so the alternative stays open. A unit that prints one against a filter would answer it in four minutes, which is a shelf question rather than a measurement one.
separated_by.what_was_ruled_out_instead: The third reading this alternative used to carry -- one stored list of frequencies with a printed range naming a window of sixteen into it -- is gone. It predicted that the entry the mid range puts at 279 would come back at 279 on any range whose window reaches it, and on 250 - 8k it comes back at 325 through one filter and 324 through another.

alternatives.reading: The three entries are 200, 250 and 315 and the filter built from them does not peak there. A table entry of this period is a set of coefficients rather than a frequency, so what is stored is already the filter -- and a section whose response below 300 Hz is not the peaking biquad the model renders would put its top somewhere else while the entry behind it is exactly the named one.

separated_by.observable: Whether the fitted position moves with the width byte at the bottom of the frequency byte's range, where at the middle of it it does not.
separated_by.divergence: 0.15 octaves, which is how far below the named series the three low entries read and is what either answer has to account for
separated_by.sensitivity_here: One twelfth-octave band, 0.083 octaves. The floor is the band and not what a fit can do, because how far apart the same setting's own takes put a fitted position has not been measured anywhere in this archive -- so the run is queued against the figure that has been

predicts.the entry is where it is read: The fitted position holds within a few hundredths of an octave across the width byte's values, exactly as it does at setting 64, and stays near 179 Hz at all of them.
predicts.the section is not a biquad down there: The fitted position moves with the width byte by more than the band it is read against, because a response that is not symmetric in log frequency is read at a different place as its flanks change.

run.why_this_shape: The same sweep the width byte already has at data/units/roland-sc8850-01/efx-bands/01-00-08-where-the-eq-hinges-in-twelfths.json, with the frequency byte at 0 instead of 64. That record is the control this one is read against, so it is the one run that answers the question and nothing else has to be repeated. Only six settings because the byte answers to 0 through 4 and reads everything above as 0, which that record already showed.

alternatives.ruled_out_by: The run it asked for was made and it split the three. Sweeping the width byte with the frequency byte at the bottom moved the top 0.149 octaves, against 0.024 for the same sweep at the middle of the range -- six times the control where the margin asked for 1.8 -- and at the two narrowest widths the top landed on 198.8 and 198.6 Hz, which is the printed 200 to a hundredth of an octave. So the first entry is 200 and the filter built from it does peak there; what did not was the shape it was read through. Read again at the narrowest width the second entry moved inside the floor, from 240.3 to 240.5 against a printed 250, which is 0.056 octaves and less than one band. The third did not move at all: 279.7 at width 2, 280.1 at width 3, 279.1 at width 4. Two of the three were the width and the third is the table.

alternatives.reading: The three entries below 315 Hz really are 200, 250 and 315 and the disagreement is the reading, not the table: the largest band of a peak this wide is a coarse estimator, and the peak's top is flat enough that a tenth of a decibel moves it.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The reading it asked for was made and says the opposite. Located by a fit over the whole feature rather than by the largest band, the three entries read 179.2, 240.3 and 279.7 Hz against 200, 250 and 315 -- 0.06 to 0.17 octaves low, where the same reading puts every entry above them inside a fifth of a band of the model. It is not scatter in the fit: the other mid section, which shares nothing with this one but the table, reads 179.1 Hz at the same setting, and the same takes read at a third of an octave instead of a twelfth put the low group 0.13 octaves out rather than 0.15. It is not the feature's width being read as its place either: the width byte of this section moves the fitted position by 0.024 octaves across every value it answers to, while moving the window that position is fitted over from four bands to forty-nine.

alternatives.reading: Thirty-two entries at equal ratios, four settings each.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It puts settings 0 and 4 in different entries and settings 8 and 12 in different entries. The reading tells neither pair apart, and the pairs are the settings the run asked precisely because four apart is where a finer table would show.

alternatives.reading: Eight entries at equal ratios, sixteen settings each.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It puts settings 0 and 8 in one entry. The reading tells them apart by five bands.

alternatives.reading: No table: the printed ends of a ratio scale over all 128 settings.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It gives every setting its own frequency, so settings 0 and 4 and settings 8 and 12 are all distinct. The reading tells neither pair apart. It is also two bands out at seven of the twelve settings, where the winner is exact.

alternatives.reading: No table: the printed ends of an evenly divided line in hertz.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It is 1.75 octaves out in the middle of the byte, which is twenty-one bands.

refuted_by: Two settings inside one of these entries returning frequencies the run tells apart, or two settings across an entry boundary returning frequencies it does not. Either is measurable at settings 4 through 12 of any slot printed with a frequency range. Or a slot on the same printed range whose readings do not land on this series at all, which would make the table a property of the type rather than of the range.

stimulus: A held note through the effect, its takes read as the energy of each twelfth octave against the run's own flat repeats.
domain.outside: Every printed frequency range except 200 - 6.3k, and every type except 01 00. The range that holds twenty third octaves rather than sixteen is the one this claim most expects to behave differently and it has not been measured. Which setting selects Bypass, on the fourteen ranges that print it. The two shelf corners of this same type, printed 200/400 and 4k/8k: a page's shelf frequency and a measurement of one are not defined at the same point, so those slots are not evidence here. The width of what sits at the frequency, which is a separate byte. Any setting between the twelve asked.

residual.unit: octaves between the band the model peaks in and the band the unit peaks in
residual.why: Zero at every entry but one under the band reading: the model's rendered profile peaks in the unit's own band at fifteen of the sixteen. The one it misses is the third, by two bands. The residual still leans, and outside that entry the lean is a bias of a median 0.030 octaves with the unit always below the model -- every value of which is inside what one band resolves, which is why it shows as a lean and not as a point of breakdown.

also_read_as.unit: octaves between where a fit puts the model's peak and where it puts the unit's
also_read_as.why: The same rendering and the same records, located by a fit over the whole feature instead of by the largest band. The winner, the ranking and the verdict are the same under both, and the entry that misses is the same entry: 0.167 octaves read one way and 0.180 the other.

gross.why: The median residual over the span the effect commands, taken as the worst of the records scored. A rejection bound and not a target: below it the residual is reported and never optimised, because no candidate is decided by it.

what_moved_the_verdict.why: Two records that sweep the byte inside its third entry alone were added to the set. The model puts that entry where the printed series does and the unit does not, so the residual is the same 0.167 octaves at every setting of them -- and a record that deliberately moves the byte inside one entry has almost no span of its own for that to be a share of. On 01-00-07-the-entry-that-is-not-printed-in-twelfths.json the span is 0.250 octaves and the median residual is 0.1668, which is 0.668 of it against a ceiling of 0.2. The gross gate had passed at 0.067 and now fails.
what_moved_the_verdict.what_is_new_in_it: Nothing about the unit. The entry that misses is the same entry, by the same 0.167 octaves, and no reading of any byte changed. What changed is that the archive now holds a record whose whole span is inside that entry, so the one departure this class has is being asked to be a small share of a small number.

what_this_does_not_close.why: They read 0.06 to 0.17 octaves below where the named series puts them, at both addresses, at two band widths and under both readings of where a feature sits. That is the breakdown, it is why the verdict is not `reproduces`, and it is the second alternative above. What it is not is the reading: the run that would have shown that has been made and shows the opposite.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: Whether the section is still a peaking biquad down there. Everything measured so far says the number belongs to the unit and not to the instrument -- two sections that share nothing but the table agree at setting 0 to 0.0008 octaves, the figure survives a fourfold change in band width, and the width byte moves the fitted position by 0.024 octaves while moving the window it is fitted over twelvefold. What is left is that a table entry of 200 Hz is right and the filter built from it does not peak at 200 Hz, which nothing here separates from an entry that is not 200 Hz. Sweeping the width byte with the frequency byte at 0 separates them: a fitted position that moves with the width is a section not behaving like a biquad, and one that holds is an entry that is where it is read.

what_this_does_not_close.what: The other thirty-four slots the page prints a frequency range against.
what_this_does_not_close.why: Six others are printed 200 - 6.3k, at five other types, and would be this same table if the printed range is what chooses it -- which is the whole of what `chosen_by` in the model asserts and none of it is measured. Twenty-eight are printed with other ends. One of those, 100 - 8.0k, brackets twenty third octaves, which a stride of eight cannot reach; six of the thirty-six slots carry it and every one of them is a phaser's manual frequency. None of the thirty-four has been measured.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: One efx-bands sweep of a slot printed 100 - 8.0k at nine settings, which is the first alternative above and is queued. It answers two things at once: whether the entries are the named series, and whether a table that will not divide the byte by a power of two takes a stride of six and leaves the last eight settings on its last entry.

what_this_does_not_close.what: Whether the Q byte indexes its printed table the same way.
what_this_does_not_close.why: The page prints five values against it and the equaliser model fits five entries, which is the same shape. But the fitted entries are close to half the printed ones for four of the five and not for the fifth, which is a definition question about what Q means on each side rather than a table question, and it is not answered by anything here.
what_this_does_not_close.what_would: Nothing new to measure. The five entries were already read at every setting; what is missing is a statement of which bandwidth definition the printed figures are, and that is a reading of the page.

what_this_does_not_close.what: Why the third entry is 279. Nothing here says whether it is a wrong constant in a table of third octaves, a right constant in a table of something else, or a coefficient set that was computed correctly for a frequency this reading is not measuring.
what_this_does_not_close.bounded_by: It is 0.18 octaves from 315 and 0.21 above the entry below it, read at three widths, at four bytes inside its own entry, at both mid sections and under both readings of where a feature sits. The reading resolves 0.083 octaves, so the disagreement is twice what the reading can be wrong by and the entry itself is not in doubt.

what_this_does_not_close.what: Whether every unit of this model holds 279 there. One unit was measured and a constant in one machine's ROM is a fact about that machine.
what_this_does_not_close.bounded_by: Nothing in this archive can bound it. It needs a second unit, which is a shelf question rather than a measurement one.

what_this_does_not_close.what: The offset that every entry shares. The unit reads below the rendered model at all sixteen, by a median 0.030 octaves and never more than 0.070 outside the third entry, and the sign never changes.
what_this_does_not_close.bounded_by: Every one of those is inside the 0.083 octaves one twelfth-octave band resolves, so no entry is individually in question -- but a bias that never changes sign is not the reading being noisy, and it is why the residual still leans and the class still breaks down. Separating a bias in the rendering from a bias in the unit needs the model rendered at a second sample rate, which is not a measurement of the unit.

what_this_does_not_close.what: What the phaser's manual table holds. Its own entries were not recovered and this claim does not extend to that address.
what_this_does_not_close.bounded_by: Four notches are in the record with their positions at nine settings, so a later reading that can account for a moving comb has the takes it needs. Nothing here says the manual is or is not a table.

what_this_does_not_close.what: Whether a record swept inside one entry of a table should carry the gross gate. The rule that sets a record aside as a null is a span of no more than twice the run's floor, and it was chosen where this type's records left a clear gap -- every ratio below 1.6 or above 6. The record added here sits at 3.0, in the gap, so the reason the figure was said not to decide anything no longer holds on this type.
what_this_does_not_close.bounded_by: It decides one verdict and no reading. The residual, the entry that misses, the ranking and the runner-up are what they were; only the share the gross gate takes of a 0.25 octave span has moved. Nothing here changes the rule, because a threshold moved after seeing what it did to a result is not a threshold.

a_note_on_what_it_replaces: That claim's sentence already says a centre moves for every eighth value of its byte, and its model does not: the model carries the twelve settings the run asked and interpolates between them, which is the measurement wearing the clothes of a law. This is the same sentence held against a catalogue instead of asserted, and with the entries named. Nothing about the chain around it changes -- the model here is that model with one map swapped, so that the residual answers one question.
a_note_on_what_was_left_out: The first pass over this class scored the same five candidates as whole band profiles in decibels and returned `equivalent_under_this_test`: every candidate passed the gross gate and none leaned. That was not the candidates agreeing. Sliding a peak of this width by a sixth of an octave costs a decibel or two on its flanks and nothing at its top, so the residual in decibels stayed under the run's own floor for candidates that were two bands out at every setting -- and a residual that is the same size everywhere does not lean, so the gate that catches a wrong structure could not catch a wrong place either. The reading was changed, not the gate's threshold: where the feature sits is what the byte moves, and the record already published it. The reading it was changed to was then changed again, and this is the second half of the same lesson. The largest band is quantised to a band, so a peak halfway between two of them cannot be read closer than half a band however good the takes are, and on a broad feature a tenth of a decibel decides which of the two it is: the width byte above moves it two bands without moving the feature at all. A fit over the whole feature is not quantised and does not do that -- and it has a bias the largest band does not, because a symmetric curve fitted to a feature whose flanks are not symmetric tops out towards the longer one. Neither reading is the better one, which is why the record now publishes both, and why what was done here was to score the same candidates twice rather than to swap one reading for the other. The finding is what survived both.

a_readout_beside_the_claim.what: The sixteen entries as this run read them, in hertz, at the narrowest width the section has.
a_readout_beside_the_claim.not_a_candidate: This is a readout and it is not in the ranking, because a table with a free entry per setting cannot come out wrong and would win on a residual that means nothing. What is claimed above is the named series, which could have come out wrong at any of sixteen entries and came out wrong at one. What is published here is what a reader downstream needs in order to render the section, including the entry the series does not account for.

read_at.located_by: a curve fitted over the whole feature, in twelfth octaves

another_printed_range.what_was_asked: 01 42's pre-filter cutoff, printed 250 - 8k. That range starts one third octave above the mid range's 200, so its second entry is the same element of a stored list as the mid range's third -- the one that came back at 279.1 Hz where the series says 315.
another_printed_range.what_it_settles: A printed range gets its own series. The second entry reads 325.2 Hz through the low-pass and 324.2 through the high-pass -- 0.0044 octaves apart from each other, and +0.046 from the printed 315 against +0.221 from the 279.1 the mid range put at the same element. One stored list windowed by the printed ends would have returned that number here and it did not, by 0.22 octaves against a reading that resolves 0.083. So the entry the mid table puts at 279 is a wrong constant in that range's own series, and not a number every range shares.

the_rest_of_the_range.read_as: Eleven settings across the range, one inside each of seven entries and four inside the first four. A corner has no vertex to fit, so it is read where the deviation crosses three decibels, interpolated between the two bands either side. That is a coarser reading than a peak's and it says so: the scatter here is twice what the mid table's was.

another_printed_range.how_far_this_widens_the_claim: To a second type and a third address, and to a printed range this claim had never been held against. What the claim says about a frequency byte is now measured on 01 00's two mid sections and on 01 42's pre-filter.

the_run_that_could_not_read.what_was_asked: A phaser's manual frequency, on 100 - 8.0k -- the one printed range this unit has whose ends bracket a number of third octaves other than sixteen, and therefore the only one on which the named series and equal ratios between the printed ends differ.
the_run_that_could_not_read.why_it_does_not_read: The type puts four notches in the band set, not one. Their ratios to each other are not constant across the sweep -- 1 : 3.36 : 7.13 at the bottom of the byte and 1 : 2.83 : 4.24 two thirds of the way up -- so there is no fixed factor between a notch and the entry behind it, and the entries cannot be recovered from where the notches are. That is measured in this record rather than assumed: the dips are in it.

the_number_it_returns_anyway.why_it_is_not_claimed: It is nearer the third octaves than the equal ratios by an octave and a third, and it would settle the alternative if a notch were a fixed multiple of an entry. The same record measures that it is not. A figure whose one assumption the run itself refuted is reported and not read.
